div.head: Cn 1020 13
div.ab: ⁊ ic wylle, þæt eal þeodscype, gehadode ⁊ læwede, fæstlice Eadgares lage healde, þe ealle men habbað gecoren ⁊ to gesworen on Oxenaforda;
⁊ ic wylle þæt eal þeodscype, gehadode ⁊ læwede, fæstlice Eadgares lage healde þe ealle men habbað gecoren ⁊ to gesworen on Oxenaforda.
[6] And ic wylle, þæt eal þeodscype, gehadode and læwede, fæstlice Eadgares lage healde, þe ealle men habbað gecoren and to gesworen on Oxenaforda.
Und ich will, dass das ganze Volk, Geistliche und Laien, fest Eadgars Rechtsverfassung halte, welche alle Männer zu Oxford erkoren und beschworen haben;
And I will that the whole people, clergy and laity, firmly keep Edgar's law, which all men have chosen and sworn to at Oxford;
And it is my will that the whole nation, ecclesiastics and laymen, shall steadfastly keep the law of Edgar to which all have given their adherence under oath at Oxford.
And it is my will that all the nation, ecclesiastical and lay, shall steadfastly observe Edgar’s law, which all men have chosen and sworn to at Oxford.
And I command that the entire populace, clergy and laity, shall faithfully obey the law of Edgar which all people have accepted and to which they swore allegiance at Oxford,
div.note: [6] Oxford: This ceremony is recorded in the entry for 1018 in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. enchantresses: The word used here is wælcyrian, the Old English term for Valkyries. It is a feature of Wulfstan’s prose that he would choose a word with pagan associations (especially for those living in the northern Danelaw) and repurpose it as the more general “enchantress” or “sorceress.”
